cards.front: What is the key structural difference between a eukaryotic cell and a prokaryotic cell?
cards.back: A eukaryotic cell has a **nucleus** and other membrane-bound organelles, whereas a prokaryotic cell has neither, and its DNA lies free in the cytoplasm.
cards.hint: Think about where the DNA is kept in each cell type.

cards.front: What is the route of a protein for export, from its synthesis to its release outside the cell?
cards.back: **Ribosomes** on the rough ER make the protein; a vesicle carries it to the Golgi apparatus, which modifies and packages it; a vesicle then fuses with the cell-surface membrane and releases it.
cards.hint: Start at the organelle that is covered in ribosomes.

cards.front: Which equation links magnification, image size and actual size, and what does each symbol mean?
cards.back: $M=\frac{I}{A}$, where $M$ is the **magnification**, $I$ is the image size and $A$ is the actual size; both sizes must be in the same unit.
cards.hint: Rearrange it to find the actual size of a cell.

cards.front: What is the job of the mitochondrion?
cards.back: It is the **site of aerobic respiration**, which makes ATP; its inner membrane is folded into cristae.
cards.hint: Think about the energy currency of the cell.

cards.front: How does the cell wall help a plant cell when it takes in water?
cards.back: Its rigid cellulose layer **supports the cell and stops it bursting**.
cards.hint: Compare with what could happen to a cell with only a membrane.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to call the cell wall the cell-surface membrane?
cards.back: The **cell wall** is a rigid, freely permeable layer outside the membrane; the cell-surface membrane is the layer that controls what enters and leaves.
cards.hint: Think about which layer does the controlling.

cards.front: What is the role of a chloroplast in a plant cell?
cards.back: It is the **site of photosynthesis**, a double-membraned organelle with stacks of flattened sacs holding chlorophyll.
cards.hint: Think about the green pigment inside it.

cards.back: A **small, circular loop of DNA**, separate from the main DNA, found in many prokaryotic cells.
cards.hint: Compare it with the circular DNA in the nucleoid.

cards.front: Why is a stain used when viewing cells with a light microscope?
cards.back: Living cells are mostly transparent, so a **stain** binds to particular structures and increases their contrast.
cards.hint: Think about how a living cell looks before any treatment.

cards.front: Why does enlarging an image not always reveal more detail?
cards.back: **Resolution** limits the detail that can be seen, so if resolution is poor, extra magnification shows no more detail.
cards.hint: Magnification only makes things bigger, so ask what limits what you can separate.

cards.front: Which microscope can show ribosomes, and why can it do so?
cards.back: An **electron microscope**, because electrons have a much shorter wavelength than visible light, giving far higher resolution.
cards.hint: Compare the wavelength of the light or beam used by each microscope.

cards.front: A cell nucleus measures 24 mm in a photograph taken at ×1200. What is its actual diameter?
cards.back: $20\,\mu\mathrm{m}$, from $A=\frac{24\,\mathrm{mm}}{1200}=0.020\,\mathrm{mm}$, then multiplied by 1000 to convert to micrometres.
cards.hint: Convert both sizes to the same unit before dividing.

cards.front: A cell with an actual diameter of 40 µm is viewed at ×500. What is its image diameter in mm?
cards.back: $20\,\mathrm{mm}$, since $40\,\mu\mathrm{m}\times500=20\,000\,\mu\mathrm{m}$, which is divided by 1000 to give millimetres.
cards.hint: Rearrange the magnification formula to find image size.

cards.front: How is an eyepiece graticule used to measure the size of a real specimen?
cards.back: First **calibrate** it against a stage micrometer, a slide with a ruler of known length; then count the graticule divisions across the cell.
cards.hint: Think about what reference you need before you can measure anything.
